articles.title: Brickbat: Sticky Fingers
articles.content:
Fairfax County, Virginia, police officer Scott Abram was charged with two counts of misdemeanor shoplifting for stealing merchandise from two Target stores. Police say that while using the self-checkout at a Target in Burke, Abram scanned a cheaper item's barcode to pay less for another item, then left the store with both products despite only paying for one. Abram was in uniform and on duty at the time. Police say he had committed a similar theft at a Target in Springfield the day before, while off duty. A 23-year veteran of the Fairfax County Police Department, Abram chose to retire rather than face termination. Each charge is a misdemeanor that can carry up to 12 months in jail and a $2,500 fine if convicted.

The post Brickbat: Sticky Fingers appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: Second Amendment Roundup: Saving Lives at Silver Rail Elementary
articles.content:
On October 15, I published a post arguing that true "sensitive places" where guns are banned must have armed protection. The same day, a murderer broke into a "gun-free-zone" school in Oregan and began shooting children and teachers. A dad of two girls at the school just happened to be driving by and grabbed his pistol, rushed into the school, and "neutralized" the killer with several shots. He was a concealed pistol licensee.
Silver Rail Elementary School is a public school in the Bend-La Pine Schools District with roughly 400 students, kindergarten through fifth grade, and approximately 40 staff members. It is located in Bend, Oregon. On October 15, a 16-year-old former special-needs student threw a shotgun over a fence outside the school and then scaled the fence. A passerby verbally confronted the teenager, who fired three shots at his truck. The driver called 911 at 12:59 p.m.
Kaylub Giamanco, a concealed pistol licensee, was also passing by when he saw the intruder shoot at the truck and then shoot the glass panes on two double doors to get inside the school. He reached for his .40-caliber pistol and rushed in through the same door. But the killer had already shot and killed three boys and a teacher and wounded another boy and a teacher. Another teacher threw a phone at the suspect, tackled him, and attempted to disarm him. As they struggled, Giamanco entered the room and shot the teen several times, killing him.
The killer fired as many as 15 rounds from a Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, which his mother had legally purchased. He had 44 more shotshells on his person and in his backpack. His devastation would have been far worse had not Giamanco intervened.
Besides a round in the chamber, the Maverick 88 shotgun holds either five or seven rounds in the magazine, depending on the model. Manufactured by Mossberg, the shotgun is typically used for protection and for hunting. It would not be an "assault weapon" under any of the laws that ban them, which exempt pump-action firearms.
Police arrived on the scene at 1:02 p.m. after being advised that the suspect had already been shot by a community member who had pursued the gunman. An armed citizen had ended the tragedy minutes before police could arrive. For the above, see ABC news account here.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek reacted to the event as follows: "To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well."
Just last year, Governor Kotek signed S.B. 243, the Community Safety Firearms Act, which her press release said "will help prevent mass shooting events in Oregon." "This matters to every parent dropping their kid off at school," in her words.
As revised by S.B. 243, Oregon law makes it a felony to possess a firearm in a public building, but if the building is a school, it is an affirmative defense that the person has a concealed handgun license, in which case it is a misdemeanor. ORS 166.370(1), (3)(g). However, a district school board "may adopt a policy providing that the affirmative defense … concerning persons licensed to carry a concealed handgun … does not apply to the possession of firearms on the grounds of the schools controlled by the board." ORS 166.377(1). A board that adopts the policy must "Post a clearly visible sign, at all normal points of entry to the school grounds subject to the policy…." Id.
The only effect of this policy is to criminalize a concealed handgun licensee from possession of a handgun at a school. It was already an offense for a member of the general public to possess a firearm at a school. Given that murder was already illegal, one would not expect a person intent on homicide to be dissuaded by a sign.
Only 25 of the 197 school districts in Oregon have adopted this policy, one of them being the Bend-La Pine School District. That policy prohibits school staff members, such as the teacher who threw her phone at the attacker, from being armed even if they are concealed pistol licensees.
It also means that the brave community member who entered the school and ended the carnage would have violated the law, but for a "choice-of-evils" justification defense. It was an emergency measure to avoid an imminent injury of such gravity that the desirability and urgency of avoiding the injury outweighed the desirability of avoiding the injury sought to be prevented by the statute defining the offense (ORS 161.200). Likewise, his use of deadly force was justified as the defense of third persons from what he reasonably believed to be the use of unlawful physical force (ORS 161.209). Those two provisions were held to warrant an adequate jury instruction in State v. Taylor (Ore. App. 1993), which was a self-defense case.
The lessons to be learned here are timeless. Thomas Jefferson and other of our Founders recognized the wisdom of Cesare Beccaria, who wrote in On Crimes and Punishments (1764):
The laws that forbid the carrying of arms … disarm those only who are neither inclined nor determined to commit crimes. Can it be supposed that those who have the courage to violate the most sacred laws of humanity … will respect the less important and arbitrary ones, which can be violated with ease and impunity…. Such laws make things worse for the assaulted and better for the assailants; they serve rather to encourage than to prevent homicides, for an unarmed man may be attacked with greater confidence than an armed man.
The post Second Amendment Roundup: Saving Lives at Silver Rail Elementary appeared first on Reason Magazine.

articles.title: France's Welfare State Is Finally Imploding
articles.content:
This week, editors Peter Suderman, Katherine Mangu-Ward, Nick Gillespie, and Matt Welch discuss the riots engulfing France and whether the country's increasingly unsustainable welfare state has made it ungovernable. They examine competing claims that immigration and austerity are fueling the unrest, the political gains being made by the French right, and why even modest pension reforms provoke fierce resistance.
The conversation turns to the United States, where President Donald Trump's tariffs are losing support among blue-collar voters and Republicans are struggling in traditionally conservative areas like Ohio. The panelists then discuss the abrupt departure of White House press secretary Katie Zacharia after just five days on the job. Later, they examine Sen. Elizabeth Warren's (D–Mass.) opposition to a proposed $45 billion merger involving McCormick and Unilever. Finally, a listener asks why libertarians don't follow the Democratic Socialists of America's example by trying to reshape the Republican Party from within.

articles.title: Justice Department Will Investigate Conditions at D.C. Jail After Years of Reports of Filth and Neglect
articles.content:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced Monday that it will investigate living conditions inside the Washington, D.C. Jail following years of reports of filth, medical neglect, and brutality.
The D.C. Jail, which holds all pretrial detainees and misdemeanor offenders in the District of Columbia, was the subject of an unflattering 2016 Reason cover story, "How Not to Build a Jail," describing how wretched conditions had persisted there for more than a century. Lawsuits, audits, and media investigations have all documented persistent civil rights problems. The jail gained additional infamy for holding pretrial detainees and convicted defendants who were prosecuted for their role in the January 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol Building.
The Justice Department received numerous allegations of excessive force, inadequate medical care, unsanitary living conditions, and malnutrition inside the jail, according to a department press release. The investigation will determine if D.C.'s Department of Corrections has a pattern or practice of violating prisoners' constitutional rights.
"The Constitution protects the rights of every incarcerated American, including those held in custody in our nation's capital," Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon said in a DOJ press release. "We are committed to upholding our federal civil rights laws so that no inmate is confined in unconstitutional conditions or subject to unconstitutional mistreatment at the District of Columbia Department of Corrections."
Last week, six current and former D.C. Jail inmates filed a class-action lawsuit alleging they found dead mice and cockroaches in their food.
Five different D.C. Jail inmates filed another lawsuit in September alleging guards failed to stop or adequately respond to a man in the jail's mental health unit from starting an electrical fire.
In 2021, the U.S. Marshals Service transferred roughly 400 inmates out of the D.C. Jail after a surprise inspection reported unacceptable living conditions, including guards withholding water and food from inmates as punishment.
A week before that inspection, a federal judge held the D.C. Department of Corrections in contempt for repeatedly failing to turn over the medical records of a January 6 defendant who had been waiting for months for a scheduled wrist surgery.
The antiquated jail, opened in the 1970s, has numerous structural problems, but plans to replace it have stalled. In the meantime, the Justice Department's Civil Rights Division will write a report to add to the top of the pile.
